q: In 1896, Henry Becquerel discovered that uranium salts emit radiations which affect photographic plates and cause ionization.
e: True. Becquerel saw uranium salts fog plates and ionize air in 1896. The year 1896 belongs to this fact, not a nearby discovery date.

q: The radiations are emitted from the nucleus of uranium atoms and are of four types; namely alpha, beta, gamma and delta rays.
e: False. The right claim is this: The radiations are emitted from the nucleus of uranium atoms and are of three types; namely alpha, beta and gamma rays. Gamma decay dumps excitation energy as a photon; Z and A stay put. The printed line wrongly says the radiations are emitted from the nucleus of uranium atoms and are of four types; namely alpha, beta, gamma and delta rays.

q: The emission of some or all of alpha, beta and gamma rays from the nucleus of an unstable atom is called radioactivity.
e: True. Radioactivity is nuclear: an unstable nucleus emits alpha, beta, or gamma. Gamma rays from the nucleus of an unstable atom is called radioactivity.

q: Of all 92 elements which exist in nature, all heavy elements with atomic number greater than 83 are stable.
e: False. The right claim is this: Of all 92 elements which exist in nature, only a few heavy elements with atomic number greater than 83 are radioactive or unstable. Radioactivity is nuclear: an unstable nucleus emits alpha, beta, or gamma. The printed line wrongly says of all 92 elements which exist in nature, all heavy elements with atomic number greater than 83 are stable.

q: Radium and polonium were discovered by Marie Curie.
e: True. The Curies isolated radium and polonium from pitchblende and named radioactivity. Marie Curie is the name attached to this result.

q: Radioactive elements can only be found in nature and cannot be artificially produced.
e: False. The right claim is this: Radioactive elements can also be artificially produced using nuclear reactors and particle accelerators. Radioactivity is nuclear: an unstable nucleus emits alpha, beta, or gamma. The printed line wrongly says radioactive elements can only be found in nature and cannot be artificially produced.

q: Alpha decay is a process in which an atomic nucleus emits an alpha particle and transforms into a different atomic nucleus, with mass number reduces by four and atomic number reduces by two.
e: True. Nuclear changes happen in the nucleus, not in the electron cloud of chemistry. With mass number reduces by four and atomic number reduces by two.

q: An alpha particle is a hydrogen nucleus.
e: False. The right claim is this: Alpha decay (alpha decay) is a process in which an atomic nucleus emits an alpha particle and transforms into a different atomic nucleus, with mass number reduces by four and atomic number reduces by two. Nuclear changes happen in the nucleus, not in the electron cloud of chemistry. The printed line wrongly says an alpha particle is a hydrogen nucleus.

q: Beta-minus decay is a process in which a neutron in an atomic nucleus changes to a proton with the emission of an electron and an antineutrino.
e: True. In metals the mobile carriers are electrons, drifting opposite the conventional-current arrow. To a proton with the emission of an electron and an antineutrino.

q: In beta-minus decay, the mass number remains unchanged but atomic number decreases by one.
e: False. The right claim is this: In gamma decay, the atomic number and mass number of the parent and daughter nuclei remain unchanged. Gamma decay dumps excitation energy as a photon; Z and A stay put. The printed line wrongly says in beta-minus decay, the mass number remains unchanged but atomic number decreases by one.

q: Beta-plus decay is a process in which a proton in an atomic nucleus changes to a neutron with the emission of a positron and a neutrino.
e: True. Beta-plus turns a proton into a neutron, a positron, and a neutrino. To a neutron with the emission of a positron and a neutrino.

q: The existence of positron was theoretically predicted by Anderson in 1931 and experimentally detected by Dirac in 1932.
e: False. The right claim is this: The existence of positron was theoretically predicted by Dirac in 1931 and experimentally detected by Anderson in 1932. Beta-plus turns a proton into a neutron, a positron, and a neutrino. The printed line wrongly says the existence of positron was theoretically predicted by Anderson in 1931 and experimentally detected by Dirac in 1932.

q: Positron, the antiparticle of electron, has the same mass and same magnitude of electric charge as an electron; but positron is positively charged.
e: True. In metals the mobile carriers are electrons, drifting opposite the conventional-current arrow. But positron is positively charged.

q: Neutrino, a fundamental particle as an electron, has a positive charge and a large rest mass.
e: False. The right claim is this: Neutrino, a fundamental particle as an electron, has no charge and negligibly small rest mass. In metals the mobile carriers are electrons, drifting opposite the conventional-current arrow. The printed line wrongly says neutrino, a fundamental particle as an electron, has a positive charge and a large rest mass.

q: For a nucleus to be stable, there must be an appropriate ratio of protons and neutrons.
e: True. Nuclear changes happen in the nucleus, not in the electron cloud of chemistry. Be stable, there must be an appropriate ratio of protons and neutrons.

q: If a nucleus has excess protons, beta-minus decay takes place.
e: False. The right claim is this: If a nucleus has excess neutrons, beta^- decay takes place. Nuclear changes happen in the nucleus, not in the electron cloud of chemistry. The printed line wrongly says if a nucleus has excess protons, beta-minus decay takes place.

q: In gamma decay, the daughter nucleus resulting from alpha or beta decay is left in an excited state and it can then decay to a lower energy state by emitting a gamma ray photon.
e: True. Nuclear changes happen in the nucleus, not in the electron cloud of chemistry. Decay to a lower energy state by emitting a gamma ray photon.

q: In gamma decay, the atomic number and mass number of the parent and daughter nuclei change significantly.
e: False. The right claim is this: In gamma decay, the atomic number and mass number of the parent and daughter nuclei remain unchanged. Gamma decay dumps excitation energy as a photon; Z and A stay put. The printed line wrongly says in gamma decay, the atomic number and mass number of the parent and daughter nuclei change significantly.

q: Photons are massless and move at the speed of light in vacuum.
e: True. Einstein's 1905 photon is the particle side of light, energy hf. Photons are massless and move at the speed of light in vacuum.

q: The energy of a photon is directly proportional to the wavelength of the electromagnetic radiation associated with it.
e: False. The right claim is this: The energy of a photon is inversely proportional to the wavelength of the electromagnetic radiation associated with it. Einstein's 1905 photon is the particle side of light, energy hf. The printed line wrongly says the energy of a photon is directly proportional to the wavelength of the electromagnetic radiation associated with it.

q: Alpha rays consist of helium nuclei, positively charged particles with a charge of +2e.
e: True. Charge is conserved; it is what a current carries and what a capacitor stores on its plates. Alpha rays consist of helium nuclei, positively charged particles with a charge of +2e.

q: Alpha rays cannot be deflected by electric and magnetic fields.
e: False. The right claim is this: Gamma rays cannot be deflected by electric and magnetic fields. Gamma decay dumps excitation energy as a photon; Z and A stay put. The printed line wrongly says alpha rays cannot be deflected by electric and magnetic fields.

q: Alpha rays are the most ionizing and the most penetrating of the three rays.
e: False. The right claim is this: Alpha rays are the most ionizing of the three rays. Alpha decay throws out a helium nucleus, so A drops by 4 and Z by 2. The printed line wrongly says alpha rays are the most ionizing and the most penetrating of the three rays.

q: Beta rays consist of either electrons or positrons moving with varying speeds.
e: True. Beta-plus turns a proton into a neutron, a positron, and a neutrino. Beta rays consist of either electrons or positrons moving with varying speeds.

q: Beta rays are more ionizing than alpha rays.
e: False. The right claim is this: Alpha rays are the most ionizing of the three rays. Alpha decay throws out a helium nucleus, so A drops by 4 and Z by 2. The printed line wrongly says beta rays are more ionizing than alpha rays.

q: Beta rays can be stopped by a few millimetres of aluminium.
e: True. Beta rays can be stopped by a few millimetres of aluminium.

q: Gamma rays are electromagnetic waves like light and X-rays, but have much longer wavelengths.
e: False. The right claim is this: Gamma rays are electromagnetic waves like light and X-rays, but have much shorter wavelengths. Gamma decay dumps excitation energy as a photon; Z and A stay put. The printed line wrongly says gamma rays are electromagnetic waves like light and X-rays, but have much longer wavelengths.

q: Gamma rays have no charge and cannot be deflected by electric and magnetic fields.
e: True. Charge is conserved; it is what a current carries and what a capacitor stores on its plates. Gamma rays have no charge and cannot be deflected by electric and magnetic fields.

q: Gamma rays are the least ionizing and the least penetrating of the three rays.
e: False. The right claim is this: Alpha rays are the least penetrating of the three rays. Alpha decay throws out a helium nucleus, so A drops by 4 and Z by 2. The printed line wrongly says gamma rays are the least ionizing and the least penetrating of the three rays.

q: Intensity of gamma rays can be greatly reduced by several centimetres of lead but they are never completely stopped.
e: True. Gamma decay dumps excitation energy as a photon; Z and A stay put. Reduced by several centimetres of lead but they are never completely stopped.

q: The rate of decay of a radioactive sample is called activity.
e: True. Activity is decays per second, the rate at which particles or gamma rays leave the sample. The rate of decay of a radioactive sample is called activity.

q: SI unit for activity is curie (Ci).
e: False. The right claim is this: SI unit for activity is becquerel (Bq). Becquerel saw uranium salts fog plates and ionize air in 1896. The printed line wrongly says sI unit for activity is curie (Ci).

q: 1 Ci is equal to $3.7 	imes 10^{10}$ event $s^{-1}$.
e: True. 1 Ci is equal to 3.7 imes 10^10 event s^-1. The power 10^10 is the conversion for this unit; a nearby prefix is a different size.

q: The rate of decay is a characteristic of the radioactive element and it is strongly affected by the temperature.
e: False. The right claim is this: The rate of decay (activity) is a characteristic of the radioactive element and it is unaffected by the temperature. Radioactivity is nuclear: an unstable nucleus emits alpha, beta, or gamma. The printed line wrongly says the rate of decay is a characteristic of the radioactive element and it is strongly affected by the temperature.

q: The half-life is defined as the time for half the atoms in a radioactive sample to decay.
e: True. Half-life is the time for half the nuclei in the sample to decay; activity halves on the same clock. The time for half the atoms in a radioactive sample to decay.

q: Radioactive decay is a deterministic process where it is possible to predict exactly when a particular atom will decay.
e: False. The right claim is this: Radioactive decay is a statistical process: it is impossible to predict when a particular atom will decay, regardless of how long the atom has existed. Radioactivity is nuclear: an unstable nucleus emits alpha, beta, or gamma. The printed line wrongly says radioactive decay is a deterministic process where it is possible to predict exactly when a particular atom will decay.

q: A tracer is a small amount of radioactive isotope introduced into a system in order to follow the behaviour of some components of that system.
e: True. Radioactivity is nuclear: an unstable nucleus emits alpha, beta, or gamma. In order to follow the behaviour of some components of that system.

q: In medicine, radioactive iodine-131 is used as a tracer to check liver function.
e: False. The right claim is this: In medicine, radioactive tracers are effectively used in diagnostic procedures, for example, to check thyroid function using radioactive iodine-131. Radioactivity is nuclear: an unstable nucleus emits alpha, beta, or gamma. The printed line wrongly says in medicine, radioactive iodine-131 is used as a tracer to check liver function.

q: In agriculture, radioisotope tracers like phosphorus-32 and nitrogen-15 are used to study the uptake of fertilizers.
e: True. A radioisotope is an unstable nuclide that decays and emits radiation. Like phosphorus-32 and nitrogen-15 are used to study the uptake of fertilizers.

q: Treatment with radiation is known as radiotherapy, and radioisotopes such as cobalt-60 and cesium-137 are widely used to treat cancer.
e: True. A radioisotope is an unstable nuclide that decays and emits radiation. Radioisotopes such as cobalt-60 and cesium-137 are widely used to treat cancer.

q: In industrial gamma radiography, alpha emitters are used to inspect metal castings or welded joints.
e: False. The right claim is this: In industrial gamma radiography, radioactive materials are used to inspect metal castings or welded joints. Gamma decay dumps excitation energy as a photon; Z and A stay put. The printed line wrongly says in industrial gamma radiography, alpha emitters are used to inspect metal castings or welded joints.

q: The ability to use radioisotopes to accurately measure thickness is widely used as thickness monitoring system in the production of sheet materials.
e: True. A radioisotope is an unstable nuclide that decays and emits radiation. Widely used as thickness monitoring system in the production of sheet materials.

q: Carbon dating is a technique developed by Albert Einstein for estimating the age of the remains of plants and animals.
e: False. The right claim is this: Carbon dating is a technique, developed by Willard Libby, for estimating the age of the remains of plants and animals. Carbon dating reads leftover carbon-14 activity in once-living remains. The printed line wrongly says carbon dating is a technique developed by Albert Einstein for estimating the age of the remains of plants and animals.

q: The half-life of carbon-14 is 5730 years.
e: True. Carbon dating reads leftover carbon-14 activity in once-living remains. The half-life of carbon-14 is 5730 years.

q: The abundance of carbon-14 in the atmosphere is essentially constant because it is continually produced by cosmic rays entering the upper atmosphere.
e: True. Carbon dating reads leftover carbon-14 activity in once-living remains. Because it is continually produced by cosmic rays entering the upper atmosphere.

q: When an animal or a plant dies, the carbon cycle stops and the carbon-14 in the remain gradually increases by radioactive decay.
e: False. After death, carbon-14 in the remains decreases by decay; it does not increase. Radioactivity is nuclear: an unstable nucleus emits alpha, beta, or gamma. The printed line wrongly says when an animal or a plant dies, the carbon cycle stops and the carbon-14 in the remain gradually increases by radioactive decay.

q: The age of igneous rocks can be estimated from the proportion of potassium-40 to argon-40.
e: True. This age of igneous rocks can be estimated from the proportion of potassium-40 to argon-40. Igneous rocks can be estimated from the proportion of potassium-40 to argon-40.

q: Gamma and neutron irradiation of seeds can be used to induce mutations to develop desired mutants that are resistant to disease.
e: True. A neutron is uncharged; fission starts when a neutron is absorbed by a heavy nucleus. To induce mutations to develop desired mutants that are resistant to disease.

q: Irradiation of food increases the microbes in food and promotes insect infestation.
e: False. Food irradiation kills microbes and insects; it does not increase them. The printed line wrongly says irradiation of food increases the microbes in food and promotes insect infestation.
